szoveg_eredeti:
African CEOs remain confident in their growth prospects despite economic uncertainty, technological disruption and an increasingly complex risk environment.

This is according to the 2026 KPMG Africa CEO Outlook, where 79% of respondents indicated that they are confident in their organisation’s growth prospects, while 72% remain optimistic about their domestic economies.

This conviction is supported by recent performance, with 86% reporting revenue growth in their latest financial year.

However, this year’s survey raises a more fundamental question: how will organisations translate ambition into execution?

The answer lies in making disciplined strategic investments in opportunities that strengthen core business capabilities, drive sustainable growth and turn confidence into measurable results.

This burden is particularly evident in the findings on Artificial Intelligence (AI). While 72% of African CEOs identify AI as a top investment priority, only 14% believe their organisation is keeping pace with or moving ahead of developments.

Subsequently, this demonstrates that a significant gap still exists between the availability of technology and the fact that many organisations are still working to build the capabilities needed to translate investment into business value.

While African organisations are investing more to close this gap, 31% successfully integrating AI into their operations; however, 27% still view this integration as a growth threat.

The real test now is whether organisations can move beyond AI experimentation to embed it meaningfully into their operations, unlock measurable business value and turn its potential into a lasting competitive advantage.

By establishing baselines, measuring results and scaling applications that work, organisations can then focus investment on practical outcomes, with efficiency and productivity offering important starting points.

The gap between AI ambition and execution is more pronounced in Africa than globally, where 72% of African CEOs identify AI as a top investment priority (79% globally).

Expectations around returns also differ with nearly half of African CEOs (48%) expecting returns within one to three years, compared with 71% globally. This is not surprising, as African businesses face both global headwinds and local economic disruptions unique to the continent.

As a result, AI investment must support clearly defined business objectives, whether improving productivity, managing costs, strengthening security or enhancing customer experience.

Essentially, organisations should measure progress by outcomes achieved, not by the number of tools adopted or pilots launched.

Such progress can only be realised, however, if organisations have the data, infrastructure, skills and operating models required to turn this investment into measurable returns.

While the tension between ambition and execution is evident across Africa, the regional findings of the 2026 Africa CEO Outlook reveal different priorities and constraints shaping AI investment and adoption.

Southern Africa has the strongest AI investment priority, at 79%, yet only 20% of CEOs believe their organisations are keeping pace.

Workforce transformation is gaining traction, with 67% redeploying staff into AI-enabled roles and 57% redesigning roles and career paths.

Therefore, realising AI’s potential will depend on developing skills, improving productivity and addressing infrastructure and vendor-related risks.

In West Africa, 63% of CEOs identify AI as a top investment priority, while 63% report a significant or transformational impact from agentic AI.

This is a strong trajectory; however, confidence to keep pace (10%) and data readiness (73%) are highly questioned. Strengthening data foundations and governance will be important to driving AI experimentation towards reliable, scalable applications.

Similar to West Africa, cost and data readiness remain key constraints, each cited by 60% of respondents. This is reflected in the focus on practical applications, including operational efficiency (64%) and threat detection and security (56%).

As a result, targeted investment in measurable business outcomes will be critical.

While 56% of North African CEOs identify AI as a top investment priority, only 29% plan to allocate more than 20% of their budgets to it.

Despite this commitment, none believe their organisations are keeping pace with AI developments. Governance and security are central concerns, with 75% focused on data governance, 69% citing ethics and 94% highlighting fraud.

Investment in skills, robust controls and responsible AI adoption will therefore become essential to building trust and delivering sustainable value.

Despite their differences, the regional findings point to a shared challenge: turning AI investment into practical, measurable value, which extends beyond technology.

Effective AI adoption depends on reliable data, appropriate skills, and clear governance safeguards, alongside a clear understanding of how AI affects workflows and how its contribution to business performance is measured.

The opportunity is to focus on applications that solve specific problems and deliver demonstrable benefits. Improving operational efficiency, reducing costs, strengthening threat detection and making better use of information can provide a foundation for broader adoption.

Over time, successful implementation may also support improved customer experiences, new products and services, additional revenue streams and changes to business models.

This disciplined approach is especially important for African CEOs, as their organisations balance growth ambitions with the need to protect margins while still building resilience.

Investment decisions must align with business priorities, with clear measures of success and a willingness to scale proven solutions rather than pursue technology for its own sake.

The findings of the recent survey suggest that African businesses are not short of AI ambition.

The real test is whether they can close the gap between recognising the technology’s potential and embedding it effectively into their operations.

Those that combine targeted investment with strong data foundations, workforce readiness and measurable outcomes will be better positioned to turn AI into a driver of productivity, stronger earnings and sustainable growth.

Shamit Govid, AI Lead - KPMG One Africa.

**The views expressed do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Media Group.
